summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Ethernet, and how link-local and autoconfigured addresses are formed there. It also defines the link-layer address option for neighbor discovery messages. It is a proposed standard and replaces RFC 1972.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2464 defines how IPv6 packets travel in Ethernet frames and how Ethernet interfaces form IPv6 addresses. It also specifies the Ethernet address information carried in certain IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets fit into Ethernet frames and how Ethernet interfaces form IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs consistent rules for transmission over Ethernet, including the frame format, packet size, address formation and link-layer address information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts IPv6 packets in standard Ethernet frames with type code 86DD hexadecimal. It defines how an interface identifier is derived from a built-in 48-bit address and how IPv6 multicast addresses map to Ethernet multicast addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2464 obsoletes RFC 1972 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 6085 and RFC 8064 as updates.

sections.title: IPv6 over Ethernet
sections.content:
RFC 2464 specifies the Ethernet frame format for IPv6 packets, how Ethernet interfaces form link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses, and the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used by IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages on Ethernet.

The option appears in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages. The RFC replaces RFC 1972.

For this specification, Ethernet includes CSMA/CD and full-duplex subnetworks based on ISO/IEC 8802-3.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC sets rules for carrying IPv6 packets over Ethernet and forming IPv6 addresses for Ethernet interfaces. It also defines Ethernet address details in Neighbor Discovery messages.

sections.title: The Ethernet MTU
sections.content:
The default IPv6 Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) on Ethernet is 1500 octets. A Router Advertisement with a smaller MTU can reduce this size, as can manual configuration of each node.

A node must ignore an MTU option in a Router Advertisement if the value exceeds 1500 or exceeds a manually configured value. Information received from DHCP is considered manually configured by this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The default maximum IPv6 packet size on Ethernet is 1500 octets. A router or manual configuration can set a lower size, but a Router Advertisement cannot raise it above the applicable limit.

sections.title: The Ethernet Frame for IPv6
sections.content:
An IPv6 packet is carried in a standard Ethernet frame. The Ethernet header contains destination and source Ethernet addresses and a type code set to 86DD hexadecimal.

The Ethernet data field contains the IPv6 header followed by its payload. Padding octets may follow when needed to reach the link's minimum frame size.
sections.plainLanguage: The Ethernet header identifies the source and destination and marks the frame as carrying IPv6. The data field then holds the IPv6 header and payload.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
An Ethernet interface's IPv6 Interface Identifier is based on an EUI-64 value derived from its built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address. The first three octets remain the company identifier, the next two become FFFE hexadecimal, and the final three octets come from the Ethernet address.

The Interface Identifier is formed by complementing the Universal/Local bit in the first octet of that EUI-64 value. The RFC gives 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE as an example input and 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE as its Interface Identifier.

A stateless autoconfiguration prefix on Ethernet must be 64 bits long. A link-local address combines the Interface Identifier with the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface identifier is made from the built-in Ethernet address by inserting two specified octets and changing one bit. A link-local IPv6 address combines that identifier with the FE80::/64 prefix.

sections.title: Mapping IPv6 Addresses to Ethernet
sections.content:
For unicast traffic, the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery specification defines how an IPv6 address maps to an Ethernet address. RFC 2464 defines the Ethernet form of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option: its Type is 1 for a source address or 2 for a target address, and its Length is 1 in units of 8 octets. It carries a 48-bit Ethernet address in canonical bit order.

The option carries the address the interface currently responds to. This may differ from the built-in Ethernet address used to form the Interface Identifier.

For IPv6 multicast, the Ethernet multicast address begins with 3333 hexadecimal and ends with the last four octets of the IPv6 destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbor Discovery uses the option defined here to carry an interface's current Ethernet address. For multicast, Ethernet copies the last four IPv6 destination octets after the fixed 3333 hexadecimal prefix.

sections.title: Changes and Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2464 replaces the earlier 48-bit Address Token with a 64-bit Interface Identifier based on EUI-64. It also changes the required autoconfiguration prefix length from 80 bits to 64 bits; the link-local prefix is 64 bits as well.

Deriving an Interface Identifier from an Ethernet address is intended to preserve global uniqueness when possible. The RFC notes that the method does not prevent duplication caused by accident or forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC uses a 64-bit Interface Identifier and a 64-bit address prefix. The derivation aims for unique identifiers, but it cannot prevent accidental or deliberate duplicates.
